title: Big Tech's AI Bill Comes Due: Amazon and Microsoft Rewarded, Meta and Alphabet Punished
content: The season's mega-cap earnings split Wall Street along a single fault line — whether soaring AI spending is being matched by demand. Amazon jumped after AWS revenue rose 36.7% year on year, its fastest pace in 18 quarters, on second-quarter earnings of $5.75 a share and $200.6bn in revenue, while Microsoft was rewarded for 43% Azure growth; Meta slid roughly 10% and Alphabet fell 6-7% as record capital-expenditure guidance crushed free cash flow.
summary: Amazon and Microsoft were rewarded for tying heavy AI spending to demand, while Meta and Alphabet were sold off for capex that gutted free cash flow.
context:
• Investors entered the season demanding proof that roughly $725bn in planned hyperscaler infrastructure spending is demand-driven rather than speculative.

• Alphabet's report a week earlier had already sparked a sell-off, raising scrutiny on every subsequent cloud result.

• Mega-cap tech carries an outsized weight in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, so individual reactions moved the whole market.
happened:
• Amazon shares jumped about 9% after hours after AWS grew 36.7%; management lifted 2026 capex guidance to roughly $220bn.

• Meta fell about 10% as free cash flow collapsed to $784m from $8.5bn a year earlier, with revenue of $60.8bn (+28%) but EPS of $6.18 missing estimates; full-year capex was guided to $130-145bn.

• Alphabet dropped 6-7% despite 82% cloud growth as capex guidance rose to as much as $205bn and quarterly free cash flow turned negative.
implications:
• The market is now discriminating sharply between hyperscalers that link spending to visible revenue and those that cannot.

• Continued mega-cap capex underpins demand for chips, power and data-centre suppliers, but tolerance for cash-flow erosion is narrowing.

• Further disappointment from a heavyweight name could trigger broader index drawdowns given tech's concentration.
importance:
• These few names drive a large share of US index returns, so their reactions set the tone for the entire equity market.

• The results reframe the AI trade around returns on capital rather than headline spending.

• Positioning around the 'Magnificent Seven' remains crowded, amplifying volatility on any surprise.

title: European Stocks Hit Record High as Tech and Earnings Extend Outperformance
content: The pan-European STOXX 600 touched a fresh record on Friday, rising as much as 0.9% to 655.45 before easing to close near 649, capping a fourth consecutive monthly gain. A 1.7% surge in technology shares — tracking Asian peers — and a run of solid corporate results powered the advance, extending Europe's outperformance against the United States this year.
summary: The STOXX 600 hit a record and locked in a fourth straight monthly gain, led by technology shares and strong earnings.
context:
• European equities have quietly outrun US benchmarks in 2026 as investors diversify away from concentrated American tech.

• The rally came through a week of central-bank decisions and Middle East tensions, underscoring resilient risk appetite.

• Semiconductor and chip-equipment names have been the region's standout performers on global AI demand.
happened:
• Chip-related stocks led the charge, with Aixtron up around 9%, Soitec up 7%, Infineon up 5.8% and ASML gaining 2.7%.

• Teleperformance jumped 7.4% after confirming its 2026 targets, lifting the industrial goods and services sector.

• Universal Music Group slumped 25.4% — its biggest one-day loss on record — after disappointing first-half results.
implications:
• Sustained European outperformance could keep drawing global flows if US mega-cap volatility persists.

• The tech rally leaves the index more exposed to any reversal in the global semiconductor trade.

• Stock-specific blow-ups such as UMG show earnings dispersion is widening beneath the index gains.
importance:
• A record high after a four-month run signals broadening risk appetite beyond US markets.

• Europe's chip-equipment champions are a key read on the health of the global AI build-out.

• Rotation into European equities is a live theme for cross-asset allocators.

title: Asian Markets Surge on AI Optimism as Nikkei Jumps and BoJ Holds
content: Asian equities rallied hard on Friday, tracking Wall Street as strong results from Microsoft and Amazon reignited the AI trade. Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed around 4% to roughly 64,362, while South Korea's KOSPI soared amid a global semiconductor rally, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both surging. The Bank of Japan left its policy rate unchanged at 1%, its highest level since 1995.
summary: Asian stocks surged on renewed AI optimism, led by Japanese and Korean chipmakers, as the Bank of Japan held rates at a three-decade high.
context:
• Asian tech and semiconductor names are highly geared to hyperscaler capex and the global AI cycle.

• The BoJ has steadily normalised policy after decades of ultra-loose settings, hiking to 1% by mid-2026.

• Korean and Japanese memory and chip-testing firms are direct beneficiaries of AI hardware demand.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 jumped about 4% to roughly 64,362, with Advantest soaring 15.7% after lifting its annual operating-profit forecast by 35%.

• South Korea's KOSPI rallied sharply, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each climbing more than 20% at their highs.

• The Bank of Japan held its policy rate at 1%, in line with expectations, keeping borrowing costs at their highest since 1995.
implications:
• Continued hyperscaler spending should keep underpinning Asian chip and memory suppliers.

• A steady BoJ leaves the door open to further tightening if inflation stays firm, a risk for the yen carry trade.

• Heavy exposure to the AI hardware cycle makes the region vulnerable to any pullback in US tech.
importance:
• Asian chipmakers are a bellwether for global AI hardware demand and supply-chain health.

• BoJ policy shifts ripple through global funding markets via the yen.

• The scale of the moves shows how tightly regional equities are now linked to the US AI trade.

title: Gold Breaks Back Above $4,100 as US Pauses Iran Airstrikes
content: Gold pushed back above $4,100 an ounce at the end of July, with August futures opening at $4,102.40 and climbing toward $4,113, after the United States paused airstrikes on Iran overnight. The move extended a choppy stretch for bullion, which set an all-time high near $5,596 in January before retreating through the spring and summer.
summary: Gold reclaimed the $4,100 level as an easing in US-Iran hostilities and a softer dollar supported the safe-haven metal.
context:
• Gold hit a record around $5,596 in January 2026 before sliding to near $4,050 by late July.

• Middle East tensions and a weaker dollar have kept safe-haven demand elevated through the summer.

• Persistently above-target inflation has bolstered gold's appeal as a hedge even as real yields stay high.
happened:
• Gold opened above $4,100 on 31 July, with August futures at $4,102.40 and moving to $4,112.90 in early trade.

• The catalyst was an overnight US pause in airstrikes on Iran, which shifted the geopolitical risk premium.

• Bullion had traded around $4,030-$4,082 earlier in the week before the break higher.
implications:
• A softer dollar and lingering geopolitical risk could keep a floor under gold near term.

• Any renewed Middle East escalation would likely reignite safe-haven buying.

• Elevated long-end Treasury yields remain a competing headwind for non-yielding bullion.
importance:
• Gold is a key barometer of geopolitical risk and real-rate expectations.

• The metal's swings reflect how tightly commodities are trading on Iran headlines.

• Bullion's resilience amid high yields signals persistent hedging demand from investors.

title: Oil Whipsaws as Iran Tensions Spike and Fade in Days
content: Crude oil endured a violent round trip in late July. Brent climbed above $88 a barrel — extending its monthly advance beyond 20% — on renewed US-Iran hostilities and reports of tankers turning back in the Strait of Hormuz, before both benchmarks plunged more than 7% in a single session on 27 July after Washington paused strikes and Tehran said it had halted retaliation.
summary: Oil surged on a US-Iran flare-up then slumped more than 7% in a day once hostilities paused, leaving Brent volatile near $88.
context:
• WTI had fallen from above $105 in early May to near $68 in early July before rebounding over 30% on geopolitical risk.

• The Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint for roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil, magnifying any disruption fears.

• OPEC+ supply discipline had already tightened the market into the summer.
happened:
• Brent pushed above $88 and WTI above $92 at the peak as tankers were reported turning around in the Strait of Hormuz.

• Both benchmarks fell more than 7% on 27 July after the US paused strikes and Iran said it had stopped retaliating.

• Brent settled around $88.46 by 31 July, still up more than 20% on the month despite the reversal.
implications:
• Oil remains hostage to Iran headlines, with sharp two-way risk into August.

• A sustained crude spike would complicate central banks' inflation fight and pressure equities.

• Any fresh Hormuz disruption could send prices sharply higher again given thin spare capacity.
importance:
• Energy prices feed directly into headline inflation and rate expectations.

• The speed of the reversal shows how much geopolitical premium is embedded in crude.

• Oil volatility drives everything from airline and transport costs to energy-sector equity performance.

title: Crypto Slips as Risk Appetite Cools Around the Fed
content: Digital assets drifted lower into month-end as traders turned cautious around the Federal Reserve decision and jittery equity markets. Bitcoin opened around $64,724 on 31 July after sliding to roughly $63,707 earlier in the week ahead of the Fed, while ether hovered near $1,917, leaving the sector rangebound rather than trending.
summary: Bitcoin and ether slipped into month-end as caution around the Fed and wobbly equities sapped crypto risk appetite.
context:
• Crypto has traded increasingly in step with risk assets, tracking equity sentiment and rate expectations.

• The late-July Fed meeting kept traders defensive across risk markets.

• Bitcoin has spent recent weeks consolidating in the low-to-mid $60,000s after earlier volatility.
happened:
• Bitcoin slid to about $63,707 on 28 July ahead of the Fed before recovering to around $64,724 by 31 July.

• Ether traded near $1,917, edging up slightly on the final day of the month.

• Prices backed off again in Friday-morning trade as broader risk appetite stayed fragile.
implications:
• With the Fed on hold, crypto may keep taking its cue from equity swings and the dollar.

• A firmer risk backdrop could see bitcoin retest higher levels, while renewed stress would pressure it.

• Range-bound trading suggests limited fresh conviction from institutional buyers for now.
importance:
• Crypto is now a mainstream risk barometer watched alongside equities and rates.

• Bitcoin's correlation to macro events makes it sensitive to Fed and inflation surprises.

• Digital-asset moves matter for the growing base of investors holding crypto ETFs and tokens.

title: Yen Jumps on Suspected Intervention as Dollar Softens
content: The Japanese yen surged in late July, with the dollar tumbling as much as 3.3% against it on Thursday amid market talk that Tokyo had stepped into the currency market to defend the beleaguered yen. The dollar index slipped toward 100 after three straight losing sessions, while the euro held around $1.145.
summary: The yen jumped as much as 3.3% on suspected Japanese intervention, dragging the dollar index back toward 100.
context:
• The yen has been under sustained pressure as Japan's rates, though rising, remain far below US levels.

• Japanese authorities have a history of intervening to curb rapid, one-way yen weakness.

• The dollar has softened in 2026 as markets weigh the Fed's on-hold stance and US fiscal concerns.
happened:
• The dollar fell as much as 3.3% against the yen on Thursday, with USD/JPY trading around 163 as Tokyo was believed to have intervened.

• The dollar index slid toward 100 after three consecutive down sessions.

• The euro held near $1.145, off its 2026 high above $1.19.
implications:
• Suspected intervention signals Tokyo's discomfort with yen weakness, raising two-way risk in the pair.

• A softer dollar, if sustained, would ease financial conditions and support commodities.

• Further BoJ tightening could compound yen strength and unwind carry trades.
importance:
• The yen is a core funding currency, so sharp moves ripple across global carry trades.

• Dollar direction shapes returns on everything from commodities to emerging-market assets.

• Intervention risk makes USD/JPY a focal point for FX traders into August.

title: Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Cools in June — But May Not Last
content: The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure eased in June, with the headline PCE price index dipping 0.1% on the month and core PCE up just 0.1%. Even so, annual rates stayed well above target, at 3.7% headline and 3.3% core, keeping pressure on a central bank that has now held rates steady amid persistent price gains.
summary: June PCE cooled month on month, but annual inflation stayed elevated at 3.7% headline and 3.3% core, keeping the Fed cautious.
context:
• Inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, limiting room to cut rates.

• The PCE index is the Fed's preferred gauge, watched more closely than CPI for policy signals.

• Consumer spending has stayed resilient, complicating the disinflation narrative.
happened:
• Headline PCE fell 0.1% in June while core PCE rose 0.1% on the month.

• Year-on-year, headline PCE ran at 3.7% and core at 3.3%, both far above target.

• Consumer spending rose 0.3% in June, led by health care, vehicles and financial services.
implications:
• A single soft print is unlikely to shift a Fed worried inflation could reaccelerate.

• Sticky core inflation supports the case for rates staying higher for longer.

• Resilient spending keeps upside risk to prices alive into the autumn.
importance:
• PCE is the data point the Fed leans on most, so it directly shapes rate expectations.

• Persistent inflation underpins elevated bond yields across the curve.

• The trajectory of core prices is central to the timing of any future rate cuts.

title: Divided Fed Holds Rates as 30-Year Yield Hits Highest Since 2007
content: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.50%-3.75% in a divided 9-3 vote, with three regional presidents dissenting as inflation has stayed above target for more than five years. The decision pushed long-dated Treasury yields sharply higher, with the 30-year bond climbing to 5.244% — its highest level since 2007 — as investors fretted that policy may not be tight enough.
summary: The Fed held rates in a 9-3 split, driving the 30-year Treasury yield to its highest since 2007.
context:
• The Fed has kept rates on hold as above-target inflation limits scope to ease.

• A rare three-way dissent underscores deep divisions on the policy path.

• Long-end yields have been climbing on inflation persistence and fiscal-supply concerns.
happened:
• The Fed left rates at 3.50%-3.75% in a 9-3 vote, with three regional presidents dissenting.

• The 30-year yield jumped 10.5 basis points to 5.201% and hit 5.244%, the highest since 2007.

• The 10-year yield rose nearly 7 basis points to 4.671%, while the two-year eased 0.02% to 4.27%.
implications:
• Rising long-end yields tighten financial conditions and pressure rate-sensitive equities.

• A steeper curve reflects growing concern over inflation and government borrowing.

• The dissents signal the bar for cuts may be higher than markets had hoped.
importance:
• The 30-year yield at a near two-decade high lifts borrowing costs across the economy.

• Fed policy and long rates anchor valuations across every asset class.

• Bond-market moves of this scale drive volatility in equities, FX and credit alike.
